deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is the elaboration behind the curvature part (Pars secunda) of Riemann's 1861 Paris prize essay on heat conduction (Commentatio mathematica). On the previous page he worked in coordinates s_i in which the geodesics from O are straight. There a_{ij} = a0_{ij} + O(s^2) and eq. (8) gives ds^2 = ds_0^2 + (2/3) Sum d^2a/ds ds (ds_i δs_k - δs_i ds_k)(ds_j δs_l - δs_j ds_l). He then replaced the coordinate-dependent conditions by invariant ones (9)-(11). In particular (9): dd Σ a δsδs = (1/3) E, where E is defined below. He also fixed the second variations dd, dδ, δδ by the geodesic equations 2 Σ_i a_{i,k} d d s_i = -Σ p_{k,i,j} ds_i ds_j, etc.

This page, step 1 (invariant quadrilinear form). For two independent displacements d and δ, define
E := dd(Σ a_{ij} δx_i δx_j) - 2 dδ(Σ a_{ij} dx_i δx_j) + δδ(Σ a_{ij} dx_i dx_j).
With the second variations fixed by the geodesic equations, E becomes a quadratic form in the bivector p_{ij} = dx_i δx_j - δx_i dx_j:
E = Σ_{pairs (ij),(kl)} (ij,kl) p_{ij} p_{kl}.
Here (ij,kl) is Riemann's four-index symbol, i.e. the covariant curvature tensor up to a normalisation factor. The sum runs over the distinct (unordered) index pairs, 'as above'. This is the formula stated without proof in the Commentatio.

Step 2 (area element). Take two line elements ds = sqrt(Σ a dx dx) and δs = sqrt(Σ a δx δx), with cos θ = Σ a_{ij} dx_i δx_j/(ds δs). The infinitesimal triangle they span has area Δ = (1/2) ds δs sin θ. A first version, 'Flächenelement', was struck and replaced by 'Dreieck'. Hence
4Δ^2 = |dx|^2 |δx|^2 - (dx·δx)^2 (Gram determinant) = Σ_{pairs} (a_{ij} a_{kl} - a_{il} a_{jk}) p_{ik} p_{jl}.
This is the Lagrange/Binet–Cauchy identity in a general metric.

Step 3 (curvature measure).
K = -(3/8) dd(Σ a δxδx)/Δ^2 = -(1/2) E / [Σ a dxdx · Σ a δxδx - (Σ a dxδx)^2].
The two forms agree via (9): (3/8)(E/3)/Δ^2 = E/(8Δ^2) = (1/2) E/(4Δ^2). In modern terms this is the sectional curvature K(σ) = R(u,v,v,u)/(|u|^2|v|^2 - <u,v>^2) of the plane σ spanned by dx and δx.

Step 4 (programme for the justification). It remains to show that K coincides with Gauss's curvature of the surface swept out by the geodesics from O whose initial directions are α dx + β δx. This is the geodesic 2-surface tangent to σ; Riemann's 1854 definition of curvature in a surface direction.
- Put x_i = r s_i, with s_i constant along each geodesic from O and r the arc length (geodesic polar / normal coordinates).
- 'As shown above', Σ a_{ij} s_i s_j = Σ a0_{ij} s_i s_j = 1. This is the Gauss lemma.
- Fix two unit systems s0, s' and let s = α s0 + β s' (12).

The next page carries this out:
- the reduction to ds^2 = dr^2 + m^2 dφ^2 (Gauss, Disq. art. 19);
- k = -m''/m;
- at the pole, k = -m'''.

[My check] In Riemann normal coordinates, g_ij(x) = δ_ij - (1/3) R_ikjl x^k x^l. With x = t·u:
- d^2/dt^2 g(v,v) = -(2/3) R(v,u,v,u) = -(2/3) K·4Δ^2;
- so -(3/8)·(-(2/3) K·4Δ^2)/Δ^2 = K.
The constants are right.
errors: No genuine mathematical error on the page. The constants -3/8 and -1/2 are mutually consistent via (9), and correct for sectional curvature in normal coordinates.

The Gram/Lagrange identity as transcribed, with coefficient (a_{ii'} a_{i''i'''} - a_{i,i''} a_{i',i'''}) multiplying (dx_i δx_{i''} - δx_i dx_{i''})(dx_{i'} δx_{i'''} - δx_{i'} dx_{i'''}), would be wrong. The term a_{i i''} a_{i' i'''} contracts antisymmetrically and contributes 0, so one would get 2·Gram over all indices, or a non-matching value over pairs. The correct coefficient is a_{ii'} a_{i''i'''} - a_{i i'''} a_{i' i''}. Summed over ordered pairs (i<i'', i'<i''') this gives exactly 4Δ^2, and over all indices 4·(4Δ^2)/... i.e. 4·Gram. Most likely the manuscript has the correct form and the transcription misread the indices.

The step from the defining conditions to E = Σ (ii',i''i''') p p (equation at top of page) is asserted, not derived on this page. It relies on the geodesic second-variation equations of the previous page; it is correct but terse.
The identification of -(3/8) dd(Σ a δxδx)/Δ^2 with Gauss's curvature is announced as still to be proved ('nun noch nachzuweisen'). It is proved on the following page, not here.

results.modern_name: Gram determinant / Lagrange (Binet–Cauchy) identity for bivectors

results.modern_name: sectional curvature = Gauss curvature of the geodesic 2-surface tangent to the plane; Riemann normal coordinates; Gauss lemma
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1854 (definition), Gauss 1827 (polar geodesic coordinates, Gauss lemma)

deep.surprise_reason: This is Riemann's own worked derivation behind the famously terse curvature formula of the 1861 Commentatio and the 1854 lecture: normal coordinates, Gauss-lemma, sectional curvature as Gauss curvature of the geodesic surface. All results are known and credited to him. The derivation was reconstructed by Weber/Dedekind in the Werke and later by Farwell–Knee and others. The manuscript detail of the exact constants (-3/8, the 1/3 relation) is of historical interest but not a new result.

transcription_corrections: In the Gram identity the coefficient should read (a_{ι,ι'} a_{ι'',ι'''} - a_{ι,ι'''} a_{ι',ι''}), not (a_{ι,ι'} a_{ι'',ι'''} - a_{ι,ι''} a_{ι',ι'''}). The transcribed form is mathematically wrong; check the image indices.

Left side of the curvature formula: the numerator is presumably dd Σ a_{ιι'} δx_ι δx_ι' (the second variation along d of the δ-length), consistent with eq. (9). The image is hard to read; 'dd Σ a dx dx' would vanish identically under the geodesic conditions.
